titleSource: The Low-Information Diet: Cultivating Selective Ignorance

sittings.bodyEn: Lifestyle design in this chapter is output, so intake has to fall. The usual intake eats hours, darkens the mood, misses your aims, or sits outside anything you can change. Look at what you read or watched today and test whether it was at least two of those four. Selective ignorance means ignoring or redirecting anything irrelevant, unimportant, or unactionable. Most of what arrives is all three. Attention is the scarce resource, and a flood of information spends it before you can. The ration that follows is a set of limits you can keep.

terms.hook: Ignoring or redirecting information that is irrelevant, unimportant, or impossible to act on.
A standing cap on news and reading so attention stays available for output.

sittings.bodyEn: The news ration is headlines glimpsed in passing, not a paper and not a broadcast. Business email gets about one hour on Mondays, and voicemail stays unchecked while you are abroad. Results-oriented reading is at most part of one industry magazine and one business magazine each month, about four hours together. An hour of fiction before sleep is for leaving the day, not for more facts. Two fact books at once are treated as a waste, so the ration is one practical book at a time. If a public story matters, the people around you will mention it, and that mention is enough. The point of the ration is a calendar that still has room for output.

The fear is that an emergency will hit while you are silent. The chapter's claim is that emergencies stop arriving once people learn you will not answer them. Many problems shrink or vanish once you stop being the person every update must pass through, and other people are allowed to act. During a fast, the priorities from the time chapter come before filler, and spare time is a reason to stay out of the news. You can still make a serious decision without living inside the media. One vote in the chapter was made in a few hours: notes to informed friends who share your values, outside observers judging past behavior, then the debates themselves. Let capable people synthesize the pile, and spend your attention on the decision.

When you must learn a how-to, pick one account by someone who has actually done it, chosen with reader reviews, and skip spectators. Read only the pages that cover the next step, which in the chapter's own case took less than two hours. Use those pages to write specific questions, then ask practitioners by email and by phone. Talking is the skill the chapter wants back, and it beat an all-you-can-eat pile of articles. That case built a short script in about four hours and finished the actual calls and notes in less than an hour, with most people answering. The mentors came from the conversations, not from finishing every chapter of every book. Read for the action in front of you, and leave the someday pile closed.

terms.hook: Material you will use now for a specific next step, instead of a pile saved for later.

sittings.bodyEn: When reading is required, use a drill the chapter says can make you at least twice as fast, and often faster, in about ten minutes, with comprehension intact. For two minutes, trace each line with a finger or a pen as fast as you can, so your eyes stop jumping backward. For three minutes, begin and end each line on the third word in from that side, then move farther inward as it gets easy. For two minutes, take only two looks on a line, on those indented words. For three minutes, push five pages faster than you can understand, in that same form, so a normal pace resets higher. To measure, average the words in ten lines, multiply by the lines on a page, then multiply by how many pages you read in one minute. Practice the four pieces in that order before you judge the method.

Start a one-week media fast and hold it for at least five full days, all at once, because a little news is the spoonful that becomes the bag. Drop newspapers, magazines, audiobooks, and radio that is not music, and keep music. Drop news sites entirely. Limit television to one hour of pleasure each evening. Limit books to this book plus one hour of fiction before bed. Use the web only for a work task required that day, and treat a nice extra as a no. Unnecessary reading is the enemy for the week, and a blocker that locks chosen sites by the clock, by a minute cap, or by both, with a password on its settings, is how you keep the rule.

The world continues when the information cord is cut, and the fast is how you notice. At breakfast, talk with a partner or a child, or study the method you mean to use, instead of reading a paper. During the old work hours, finish the top priorities from the time chapter, and if they are done early, do the exercises in this book. The pages you are in are meant to be used now, which is why they stay allowed during the fast. Each day at lunch, and no earlier, take a five-minute news fix by asking a colleague or a waiter whether anything important happened. Stop that question once you see that the answer never changes your actions. Most people cannot remember what they spent an hour or two absorbing that morning, and the fast is supposed to make that obvious.

Before you consume anything, ask whether you will definitely use it for something immediate and important. If either word fails, skip it. Information you will forget before you can apply it is useless, which is why reading weeks ahead creates a second reading later. Follow the short to-do list and fill gaps as you reach them. That is just-in-time information, and the just-in-case pile is the habit being cut. Starting something does not require finishing it. Put down a bad article, leave a bad film, and stop when you are full, because quitting a boring or useless thing is often far better than completing it when nobody is requiring the ending.

terms.hook: Stopping a boring or useless thing when nobody requires you to reach the end.

sittings.bodyEn: For two days, ask at least two people you find attractive for a phone number, with eye contact, and attempt more if the fear is loud. The real goal is the ask, so a refusal counts as a finished rep and the number itself is secondary. If you are already partnered, use a harmless survey frame and throw the numbers away. A mall is the fast version: three asks in a row inside five minutes. Keep the script short, admit the ask is sudden, give yourself a reason you cannot linger, and give them an easy refusal, including a fake number. The chapter includes women and older readers on purpose, because the fear of asking is the target. Run one comfort challenge at a time, marked on the calendar.

Information earns a place when you will definitely use it soon for something important. The media fast is a short, strict cut so you notice that life continues, and it still allows music, one evening hour of television, and bedtime fiction. News grazing, idle web time, and a duty to finish every opening are the habits being removed. A how-to is one done-it account, only the pages for the next step, then questions to people who have done it. Emergencies shrink once people learn you are not the bottleneck. The diet exists so output has room.
sittings.prompt: When does this chapter say you should consume a piece of information?
choices: Whenever the topic sounds serious or might be useful someday
Only when you will definitely use it soon for something important
Every morning, so you stay informed before any work starts
After you finish whatever you started, because quitting is wasteful
